00:00.000–00:02.800: A male voice speaks clearly, “What is Nibbana?”

00:04.800–00:13.800: A different male voice, slightly lower in pitch, speaks: “This is peaceful. This is excellent, namely the stilling of all preparations, the relinquishment of all assets, the destruction of craving, detachment, cessation, extinction.”

00:15.800–00:18.800: A third male voice, with a questioning tone, asks: “Why don’t I see Nibbana right now?”

00:20.800–00:27.800: A fourth male voice, measured and calm, says: “So then, due to the very ignorance of the fact that it is seeing because it is looking, the dog imagines another dog there in the what?”

00:29.800–00:32.800: A fifth male voice, slightly faster, asks: “What keeps it going?”

00:34.800–00:39.800: A sixth male voice, with a reflective tone, says: “Perception. What impels one to ignore that gap is craving. It is sometimes…”

00:41.800–00:45.800: A seventh male voice, clear and deliberate, asks: “How is the sense of self constructed?”

00:47.800–01:02.800: An eighth male voice, with a narrative cadence, says: “Even if one already has no such notion, the moment one looks into a mirror, one is suddenly reminded of it, as if to exclaim, ‘Ah, here I am!’ This is the gist of what Ven. Punnamantani Putta is trying to put across through this discourse. This shows that the conceit ‘I’ arises due to the five grasping groups.”

01:04.800–01:08.800: A ninth male voice, calm and declarative, asks: “How is Nibbana attained?”

01:10.800–01:25.800: A tenth male voice, with a rhythmic, almost poetic delivery, says: “And when you’re not by it, you’re not in it. And when by it you’re not in it, then by here you’re neither here nor there nor in between. This itself is the end of suffering. (Common translation by Ireland.) When by here in the scene is merely what is seen, in the heard is merely what is heard, in the sensed is merely what is sensed…”

01:27.800–01:31.800: An eleventh male voice, with a soft, almost whispered tone, asks: “What is Nibbana like?”

01:33.800–01:38.800: A twelfth male voice, with a slightly theatrical or recitative tone, says: “They would say, ‘See, the Buddha has seen Nibbana. I am grown cool, extinguished as I am.’”

— End of audio —

00:00:02.000 --> 00:00:05.000: Speech continues: “This is peaceful. This is excellent. Namely, the stilling of all preparations, the relinquishment of all assets, the destruction of craving, detachment, cessation, extinction.”

00:00:05.000 --> 00:00:08.000: Speech continues: “When a fire is burning, if someone were to ask, ‘What is burning? What shall we say as a reply?’”

00:00:08.000 --> 00:00:11.000: Speech continues: “Those wise ones get extinguished even like this lamp. The simile of a lamp getting extinguished.”

00:00:11.000 --> 00:00:14.000: Speech continues: “The simile of the extinction of a fire is very often brought in as an illustration of Nibbana, and the Angi Vatthagotta Sutta of the Majjhima Nikaya, we find the Buddha presenting it as a sustained simile, giving it a deeper philosophical dimension.”

00:00:14.000 --> 00:00:17.000: Speech continues: “Now, when a fire burns, it does so with the help of firewood. When a fire is burning, if someone were to ask us, ‘What is burning? What shall we say as a reply?’”

00:00:17.000 --> 00:00:20.000: Speech continues: “Is it the wood that is burning, or the fire that is burning? The truth of the matter is that the wood burns because of the fire, and the fire burns because of the wood.”

00:00:20.000 --> 00:00:23.000: Speech continues: “So it seems we already have here a case of relatedness of this to that — ida-paccayata. This itself shows that there is a very deep significance in the fire simile.”

00:00:23.000 --> 00:00:26.000: Speech continues: “Nibbana is a term for the ultimate aim of the Dhamma, is equally significant because of its allusion to the going out of a fire.”

00:00:26.000 --> 00:00:29.000: Speech continues: “In the Asankhata Samyutta of the Samyutta Nikaya, as many as thirty-three terms are listed to denote this ultimate aim.”

00:00:29.000 --> 00:00:32.000: Speech continues: “But out of all these epithets, Nibbana became the most widely used, probably because of its significant allusion to the fire.”

00:00:32.000 --> 00:00:35.000: Speech continues: “The fire simile holds the answer to many questions relating to the ultimate goal.”

00:02.000 --> 00:03.000: A sharp, abrupt cut to silence — no speech, no ambient sound.

00:03.000 --> 00:05.000: A male voice begins speaking, “Perception. What impels one to ignore that gap is craving.”

00:05.000 --> 00:07.000: The male voice continues, “It is sometimes...”

00:07.000 --> 00:09.000: A brief pause — no speech, no ambient sound.

00:09.000 --> 00:11.000: The same male voice resumes, “...deep and apparent name.”

00:11.000 --> 00:13.000: He continues, “Forming name and form is a nominal form.”

00:13.000 --> 00:15.000: “It is a form only in name.”

00:15.000 --> 00:17.000: “We have to make a similar comment on the meaning of the word nibbana.”

00:17.000 --> 00:19.000: “Because of this misconception the world is in a tangle.”

00:19.000 --> 00:21.000: “Names and concepts, particularly the nouns, perpetuate the ignorance in the world.”

00:21.000 --> 00:23.000: “Therefore insight is the only path of release.”

00:23.000 --> 00:25.000: “And that is why a meditator practically comes down to the level of a child in order to understand name and form.”

00:25.000 --> 00:27.000: “He may even have to pretend to be a patient in slowing down his movements for the sake of developing mindfulness and full awareness.”

00:27.000 --> 00:29.000: “So we see that there is something really deep in namarupa.”

00:29.000 --> 00:31.000: “Even if we render it as name and form, there is an implicit connection with name as conventionally so called.”

00:31.000 --> 00:33.000: “But unfortunately this connection is ignored in the commentaries when they bring in the idea of bending to explain the word name.”

00:33.000 --> 00:35.000: “So we need not hesitate to render namarupa by name and form.”

00:35.000 --> 00:37.000: “Simple as it may appear, it goes deeper than the worldly concepts of name and form.”

00:37.000 --> 00:39.000: “Now if we are to summarize all what we have said in this connection, we may say: name in name and form is a formal name.”

It can only point to the moon and I am also not looking for the moon right at the top of the finger. The finger is far away from the moon. But the finger shows me a direction. At 00:01:00.000 — “How monks do some overreach, being troubled, ashamed, and disgusted of existence as such, some delight in non-existence. It probably means the sediments or dregs, Sanskrit ‘kshara’, of speech, namely the worldly concepts and designations which as ‘papanca-sanyasanka’, reckonings born of prolific perception, form the basis of all thoughts. In the arahant, therefore, influxes of existence as well as sediments of speech are smoked out, gone down and made extinct. This then seems to be the most plausible interpretation of the two lines in question: ‘bhavasamayassa vachikaraja vidupita attagatana santi.’ So we have garnered sufficient canonical evidence to conclude that the terms ‘vitakka’ and ‘papanca’ are particularly relevant to the life of a meditator. Also the fact that the arahatapala samadhi has been called ‘avvitaka samadhi’ shows that the conquest of thoughts is not of a temporary type, as in the case of tranquility meditation. On the other hand, it is a transcendence of a more radical type, through an insight into the relative validity of worldly concepts, their falsifying nature, and the perception of permanence underlying them. ‘Avvitaka samadhi’ is a term used to denote that state of complete emancipation of the mind by making all signs fade away, so that the whole world appears like a blotched watercolor painting, thus freeing the mind from the perception of diversity without even resorting to a perception of unity.”

—

At 00:02:18.000 — “Steadied whereon the tides of imaginings occur no more in him. The idea behind the ‘currents of tides of imaginings’ is quite often represented by the concept of ‘asava’ influx. It does not simply mean reckoning or adding up in terms of numerals. It is characteristic of language too, as we may infer from the occurrence of the expression ‘sankhanga cheti’ in many discourses. Therefore, there the reckoning meant is a particular linguistic usage. We come across a good illustration of such a linguistic usage in the ‘Maha Hatthipadopama Sutta’, where Ven. Sariputta is addressing his fellow monks.”
